ta-l1d37q3-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus mapping the structure of Peter Lombard's text: having shown that God is everywhere, the text now excludes from God two things that follow upon a creature existing in place — locality and motion. It traces Lombard's threefold division (stating the intention that the divine essence is neither moved nor local; showing that locality and motion belong to every creature, either by circumscription for bodies or by definition alone for spirits, and that only motion through time, not through place, straightforwardly belongs to spirit; then proving both are removed from God) and identifies the two questions actually pursued here: the place of an angel and its motion, since God's immutability and omnipresence were already treated in Quaestio 2, and the motion and place of bodies belongs to natural philosophy, not theology. It closes by naming the three articles: whether an angel is in place, whether one angel can be in several places at once, and whether several angels can be in one place.
concepts: locality and motion as creaturely conditions
scope of theology vs. natural philosophy

ta-l1d37q3-d1e131.summary: First objection of Article 1. Boethius states that it is the common conception among all the wise that incorporeal things are not in place. But angels are incorporeal and immaterial, as Dionysius says. Therefore angels are not in place.
claims: Boethius's dictum that incorporeal things are not in place, applied to angels (incorporeal per Dionysius), implies angels are not in place.

ta-l1d37q3-d1e137.summary: Second objection. To whatever is wholly free from position and dimension, place belongs only per accidens, as is clear with prime matter. But an angel's essence is wholly free from position and dimension, as all who call angels incorporeal hold. So place belongs to it only per accidens — and per accidens presence in place occurs only by assuming a body. Therefore, when an angel has not assumed a body, it seems not to be in place at all.
claims: An essence wholly free from position and dimension (like prime matter, and like angelic essence) is in place only per accidens, i.e. only by assuming a body.

ta-l1d37q3-d1e140.summary: Third objection, anticipating the reply that an angel is in place through its operation. Against this: whatever belongs to something through something else must belong properly to that through which it belongs — as, if an animal is in place through its body, the body itself must be in place. But being-in-place is never attributed per se to an operation. Therefore an angel cannot be in place through operation.
claims: Since operation itself is never per se said to be 'in place,' an angel cannot derive its own presence in place from its operation.
concepts: transitivity of predication through an intermediate

ta-l1d37q3-d1e144.summary: Fourth objection. If being in place belongs to an angel through operation, this holds only insofar as it operates on something in a place. But angels do not always operate on corporeal things. So at times they would be nowhere — and they cannot be said to be everywhere either, since that is proper to God alone. It would follow that angels are sometimes nowhere at all, which seems absurd.
claims: If presence in place depends entirely on an angel's current operation, an angel not presently operating on anything corporeal would be nowhere, an apparently absurd consequence.
concepts: omnipresence as proper to God alone

ta-l1d37q3-d1e147.summary: Fifth objection. If an angel is in place through its operation, then it is definitively in place, since its operation is defined and determined to a place. But some operation of God is likewise defined to a particular place, outside which he does not exercise it, as is clear in the raising of a particular dead person. It would seem to follow that God too is definitively in place.
claims: If operation-defined presence entails definitive location, then God's occasionally place-restricted operations (e.g. a particular resurrection) would seem to entail that God too is definitively located.

ta-l1d37q3-d1e150.summary: Sixth objection. The philosophers held that the operations of the separate intelligences concern things here below, yet did not say the intelligence itself is in any place; indeed Plato held that the Ideas are neither within nor outside the heavens, precisely because they are not in place (per Physics 3). Therefore angels should not be said to be in place through their operation either.
claims: Philosophical precedent (intelligences, Plato's Ideas) shows that having operative effects on located things does not by itself entail being in place, undermining the operation-based account of angelic presence.

ta-l1d37q3-d1e153.summary: Sed contra: the liturgical collect prays 'may your holy angels dwell in it, who guard us in peace.' Damascene likewise says that angels are where they operate, and this is easily proved by many other authorities.
claims: Liturgical and patristic authority (the collect, Damascene) affirms that angels dwell/are where they operate.

ta-l1d37q3-d1e159.summary: The main determination (respondeo) of Article 1, surveying three opinions. The first, held by the philosophers, denies that intelligences/angels are in place at all, on the ground that an intelligence is an essence stripped of matter that moves its sphere only as an object of desire through a soul conjoined to the sphere, never immediately operating on any body; Thomas rejects this as heretical, since faith holds that angels immediately operate around us. The second opinion holds that place is owed to the angel even with respect to its essence, and that an angel's existence is unintelligible without place, but that it is in place definitively rather than circumscriptively, since its essence, being finite (as a creature), must be determined to some place; Thomas judges this proof crude, resting on an equivocation between 'finite' as a limit of essence/power (as in 'definition') and 'finite' as a limit of dimensive quantity — the two senses bear no proportion to one another, so being finite in essence does not entail being bounded by the limits of place. He then argues that determination to a place requires some mode of application to it — by position/contact, by form, or by operation. By form, as the soul is in the body, an angel cannot be in a located thing since it is not the act of a body. By determinate position, as a point in a line, an angel is not in place, since its essence is wholly free from position. By contact — proper contact (having extremities together) cannot belong to an angel, but metaphorical contact through action (as one 'touches' by saddening someone) can. It follows that an angel can be defined to a place only through action and operation — the third opinion, confirmed by Gregory Nazianzen, who says that when we should say 'it operates here' we improperly say 'it is here.' Following this more reasonable opinion, Thomas holds that an angel, and any incorporeal substance, can be in a body or place only through an operation causing some effect in it, which happens in three ways: a spiritual substance may confer on a body something added to esse without conferring esse itself (as an angel operating on a located body, its motion, or light); it may give a body an esse other than its own (as God gives esse to all creatures, but not his own esse); or it may give a body its own esse, either as act of form (as the soul is the form of the body) or as act of hypostasis rather than form (as in Christ, where human nature was assumed to the esse of the divine person through union in hypostasis, not confusion of nature).
claims: The philosophers' view that intelligences are wholly unrelated to place or body is heretical, since faith holds that angels immediately operate around us.
The 'finite essence entails finite place' argument for angelic definitive location equivocates between two unrelated senses of 'finite' (limit of essence/power vs. limit of dimension).
An angel can be determined to a place only through operation (a kind of metaphorical, action-based contact), not through form or determinate position as bodies and points are.

Spiritual substances relate to bodies in three graded ways: conferring something added to esse (angels generally), conferring an esse other than their own (God as creator), or conferring their own esse as act of form (soul) or as act of hypostasis (the Incarnation).
concepts: esse as act of form vs. act of hypostasis

ta-l1d37q3-d1e162.summary: Reply to the first objection. Place is the name of a measure, so being-in-place properly signifies being-in-a-measure, which belongs to no incorporeal thing as being 'in place' strictly. But it can belong to an incorporeal thing to be in place in a different sense — not as in place, but as an operator is in what it operates on, or as form is in matter. Hence an angel is called 'local' only in a qualified sense, insofar as it has something analogous to a located thing, namely being determined to this place rather than that one.
claims: Boethius's dictum concerns place strictly as measure, which indeed excludes incorporeal things; angels are 'in place' only in the distinct, qualified sense of operator-in-operated, not measured-in-measure.

ta-l1d37q3-d1e166.summary: Reply to the second objection. Being in place as in place belongs to an angel only per accidens, insofar as an assumed body, or the body to which it is applied through operation, is in place; but being in place as operator-in-operated belongs to an angel even per se, insofar as it operates per se in place — just as prime matter is per se in place or in the located thing as a part, and a point is per se in place as its terminus, not as something located.
claims: Angels are in place per accidens only in the sense of 'as in place' (via a body), but per se in the distinct sense of 'as operator in what is operated on.'
concepts: per se vs. per accidens presence
prime matter and point as analogies

ta-l1d37q3-d1e169.summary: Reply to the third objection. An angel's operation is not itself in place as something located, but as the perfection of the located thing, since the operation of an agent is always the perfection of the patient, precisely as such.
claims: Operation is 'in place' only as the perfection it produces in the located patient, not as itself a located entity — dissolving the objection's demand that operation itself be shown to be in place.
concepts: operation as perfection of the patient

ta-l1d37q3-d1e172.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. Thomas does not find it problematic that an angel could exist without operating on anything in place and so not be in place at all, nor that it then be said to be nowhere — just as it is not problematic to say something is colored by no color. He adds, however, that this state is not imaginable, since imagination cannot transcend the continuum.
claims: An angel with no current spatial operation may simply be 'nowhere' without absurdity — a non-imaginable but intelligible state, since imagination is inherently bound to spatial continua while intellect is not.

ta-l1d37q3-d1e175.summary: Reply to the fifth objection. An angel is definitively in place through its operation, but God is not, because God's operation, though determined to a place insofar as it passes onto what is operated on, is not so determined insofar as it proceeds from the operator — God so operates here that he also operates elsewhere simultaneously. The angel's operation, by contrast, is defined to place in both respects, since (as will be shown in the next article) an angel does not operate elsewhere than where it currently operates.
claims: God's operation is place-determined only on the receiving end (where it terminates), never on the originating end, since God acts everywhere at once; an angel's operation is place-determined on both ends, which is why only the angel, not God, is definitively located.

ta-l1d37q3-d1e178.summary: Reply to the sixth objection. An operator need not be in, or applied to, what is operated on except with respect to what it immediately operates on. The philosophers held that the operation of an intelligence reaches things here below only mediately, through the motion of the spheres, and reaches the sphere itself only mediately, through its soul, which they said is in the sphere; it therefore follows on their own premises that the intelligence itself is wholly free of body and place — a conclusion that depends on their mistaken doctrine of mediated operation, not on a sound general principle.
claims: The philosophers' conclusion that intelligences are unrelated to place follows only because they posited a mediated chain of operation (intelligence-soul-sphere-things here); it does not show that immediate operation, as angels exercise, fails to place an agent.

ta-l1d37q3-d1e190.summary: First objection of Article 2. Every body is more determined to place than an angel is. But some body is simultaneously in several places, as the body of Christ is on several altars [in the Eucharist]. Therefore, much more can an angel be simultaneously in several places.
claims: Since even a body (more place-bound than an angel) can be in several places at once (the Eucharistic body of Christ), an angel should be able to as well, a fortiori.

ta-l1d37q3-d1e193.summary: Second objection. When an angel assumes a body, it clearly moves every part of that body immediately — otherwise the motion would be disordered, unlike the motion of a living animal. But an angel is wherever it immediately operates. Therefore the angel is in each part of the assumed body, and so seems to be simultaneously in several places.
claims: An angel's immediate motion of every part of an assumed body implies, by the operation-based criterion of presence, that the angel is simultaneously present in each of those parts, i.e. in several places.

ta-l1d37q3-d1e196.summary: Third objection. The empyrean heaven is owed to angels for the work of contemplation. But when angels operate here among us, they do not cease to contemplate. Therefore they are simultaneously here and in the empyrean heaven, and so in several places.
claims: If contemplation requires location in the empyrean heaven, and angels contemplate continuously even while operating elsewhere, they must be simultaneously present in both places.

ta-l1d37q3-d1e200.summary: Fourth objection. Every agent whose power exceeds what it operates on can also operate on something else. But an angel's power exceeds the single body it operates on. Therefore it can operate on something else too, and so can be in several places — since wherever it operates, there it is.
claims: Because an angel's power exceeds any single object it acts on, it should be able to act on further objects simultaneously and thus be present in several places at once.
concepts: excess of agent power over patient

ta-l1d37q3-d1e203.summary: First sed contra of Article 2. Damascene says that while angels are in heaven, they are not on earth; this seems to show that they are not simultaneously in several places.
claims: Damascene's statement that angels in heaven are not on earth implies angels are not simultaneously present in multiple places.

ta-l1d37q3-d1e206.summary: Second sed contra. The text under discussion states and proves that an angel is definitively in place. But what is in several places is not defined or determined to any one place. Therefore an angel is not in several places.
claims: Definitive presence (already established) is incompatible with being in several places at once, since definitive location means being determined to one place.
concepts: definitive presence as incompatible with multi-location

ta-l1d37q3-d1e209.summary: The main determination (respondeo) of Article 2, again surveying and rejecting mistaken opinions before stating Thomas's own view. Some held an angel can be in several places at once, though not everywhere like God, while a body is only ever in one place — but the masters judged this an error, since it would leave an angel neither definitively nor circumscriptively in place. Others held an angel is in an indivisible place, reasoning that place is owed to the angel's essence itself, and since that essence is indivisible, its place must be indivisible too — but Thomas attributes this error to an inability to transcend imagination, which cannot conceive anything indivisible except as having position within a continuum. Instead, Thomas holds that an angel is in one place only, but that place can be divisible or indivisible, large or small, according to whatever its operation is immediately terminated at — so if it immediately operates on a whole house, the whole house is its one place, and it is thereby in every part of that place, just as the soul is said to be in every part of the body. He stresses 'immediately': if an angel moved a stone that set many other things in motion, it need only be where the first thing moved is, just as a corporeal mover need only touch what it directly moves. The reason an angel cannot be in several places at once is that it has a finite nature and consequently finite power, and only one operation can proceed from one finite power — an operation being one precisely because it terminates in one thing operated on — so the angel's object of operation must be single. Just as a soul is not simultaneously in several bodies, an angel is not simultaneously in several places. Only God can be in several and in all places at once, because his power is infinite: though his operation is one insofar as it is identical with himself, its effects are infinite, since he is the principle giving esse and thus creating everything else added to esse — so he is present in all things not as in one thing operated on, but as in many, since even what distinguishes the things in which he operates comes from him.
claims: The 'several places but not everywhere' opinion is erroneous because it leaves the angel neither definitively nor circumscriptively located, violating the very distinction the prior article established.
The 'indivisible place' opinion mistakes the imagination's inability to conceive indivisibility except as a point-in-continuum for a metaphysical truth about angelic place.

An angel occupies exactly one place, whose size and divisibility are fixed entirely by the immediate terminus of its single operation — as with a whole house it operates on directly, or as narrowly as the single object it immediately moves.

An angel's finite power can support only one operation, and one operation terminates in only one object, so an angel cannot be in several places at once, just as a soul is not in several bodies at once.
Only God, whose power is infinite and whose single self-identical operation has infinite effects, is present in many places and all places at once.
concepts: finite power admits only one operation

ta-l1d37q3-d1e212.summary: Reply to the first objection. The body of Christ does not have, either as body or as united to divinity, the property of being in several places; rather it has this by reason of consecration and transubstantiation, insofar as the diverse breads that are transubstantiated into it are in diverse places — because the substance of bread passes into the body of Christ while the accidents remain, the quantity (and hence place) of each bread remains, and the same would occur with whatever else bread were transubstantiated into by divine power.
claims: Multi-location of Christ's Eucharistic body is not a property of the body as such or of the hypostatic union, but a consequence of transubstantiation and the persistence of bread's accidents (including quantity/place) after its substance is converted.

ta-l1d37q3-d1e215.summary: Reply to the second objection. The whole assumed body is compared to the angel as a single indivisible 'where,' inasmuch as there is one operation concerning it as a whole. Hence, although the angel is in every part of the assumed body, it need not thereby be in several places.
claims: Presence in every part of a single assumed body (via one unified operation on the whole) counts as being in one place, not several, since the whole body constitutes a single 'where' for that operation.
concepts: unity of operation defines unity of place
'where' (ubi) as indivisible relative to one operation

ta-l1d37q3-d1e219.summary: Reply to the third objection. Operation is, as it were, a medium between operator and thing operated on, and can be considered either as it proceeds from the operator or as it terminates at what is operated on. Place is owed to an angel's operation not according to its origin in the angel's own essence, which is absolute in itself, but according to the object at which it terminates; since the object of contemplation is spiritual, contemplative operation is owed no corporeal place at all. The empyrean heaven is therefore not necessary for contemplation but is assigned to it only through fittingness (congruentia), being sanctified for the glory of the blessed — much as the Church, rather than the marketplace, is said to be more fittingly the place of contemplation. It does not follow that an angel is in the empyrean heaven whenever it contemplates.
claims: Place is assigned to an angel's operation by the operation's terminus (its object), not by the origin of the operation in the angel's essence.
Since contemplation's object is spiritual, contemplative operation has no corporeal place strictly required; the empyrean heaven's association with contemplation is one of fittingness, not necessity.

ta-l1d37q3-d1e222.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. Although an angel's power exceeds what it currently operates on by an excess akin to continuous quantity (it could operate on something larger), it does not exceed it by an excess of discrete quantity, since it can operate on only one thing at a time, whether that thing be large or small.
claims: An angel's excess of power over its object is an excess of magnitude (it could act on something bigger), not an excess of number (it still can only act on one object at a time), so surplus power does not license simultaneous multiple operations.
concepts: continuous vs. discrete quantity as applied to power

ta-l1d37q3-d1e234.summary: First objection of Article 3. A body is more filling of place than a spirit. But where a body can be, an angel can be. Therefore, much more is an angel not prevented from being where another angel already is.
claims: Since bodies (which fill place more fully than spirits) do not prevent an angel from occupying their place, a fortiori another angel's presence should not prevent it either.

ta-l1d37q3-d1e237.summary: Second objection. Per Augustine, the soul is in every part of the body. Demons and angels, though they do not slip into minds, do slip into bodies, as the saints say. It seems, therefore, that an angel and a soul can be in the same place — and by the same reasoning, that an angel and another angel could be too.
claims: Since a demon or angel can co-occupy a body already animated by a soul, it seems two spiritual substances (an angel and a soul, or two angels) can occupy the same place together.
concepts: Augustine on the soul's presence in the body

ta-l1d37q3-d1e240.summary: Third objection, anticipating and rebutting the reply that co-location of two angels would be barred to avoid confusion. Against this: confusion is more repugnant to greater distinction. But created spirit is more distinguished from uncreated spirit (God) than one created spirit is from another. Yet angels, as the text states, run without any confusion within God himself wherever they are sent. It seems, therefore, that two angels should likewise be able to be simultaneously in one place.
claims: If angels can exist without confusion 'within' God — despite the maximal distinction between created and uncreated spirit — the lesser distinction between two created spirits should allow co-location without confusion even more readily.
concepts: degree of ontological distinction and confusion

ta-l1d37q3-d1e244.summary: Fourth objection. Just as an angel operates around a body, it also operates around another angel, since (per Dionysius) superior angels illuminate inferior ones. But operating around a place is what makes an angel said to be in that place; so operating around another angel should likewise mean being in that angel — and so it seems two angels can be in one place.
claims: By the operation-based criterion of presence, an illuminating angel's operation on another angel should imply that the illuminating angel is 'in' the illuminated angel, and hence that two angels can share one place.
concepts: extension of the operation-based criterion to angel-on-angel action

ta-l1d37q3-d1e247.summary: First sed contra of Article 3. As a body relates to circumscriptive presence in place, so an angel relates to definitive presence. But two bodies are not circumscribed by the same place. Therefore neither are two angels defined to one and the same place.
claims: By analogy between circumscriptive presence (bodies) and definitive presence (angels), just as two bodies cannot share a place, two angels cannot be defined to the same place.
concepts: analogy of circumscriptive and definitive presence

ta-l1d37q3-d1e250.summary: Second sed contra. One body does not have two souls, even though the soul is a spiritual substance, just as an angel is. It seems, therefore, that neither can two angels be in one and the same place.
claims: The impossibility of two souls informing one body, despite the soul's spirituality (shared with angels), suggests two angels cannot occupy one place either.
concepts: uniqueness of the substantial form (one soul per body)

ta-l1d37q3-d1e253.summary: The main determination (respondeo) of Article 3. Place can be taken properly or metaphorically: metaphorically, an angel's 'spiritual place' is God himself, who contains as place does by likeness, so that in this sense all angels — indeed all beings — are in one place, namely in God who contains all things. But the question concerns place properly so called, i.e. corporeal place, and here, following the common opinion, Thomas holds that several angels cannot simultaneously be in one place. The reason is drawn from the side of the operation by which an angel is said to be in place: since (per the Philosopher) a thing is most perfectly defined when its nature, all its consequent properties, and the resolution of all incidental doubts are shown through the definition, it must be held that it is impossible for the same thing, under the same respect, to be acted upon and moved by diverse agents if each agent is of perfect power sufficient to produce that effect — multiple agents jointly producing one effect occurs only when each is an imperfect mover acting by the power of one (as with several men pulling a ship), since a perfect agent brings its patient fully into act, leaving no further potency to be actualized by another. Since one angel, acting by the power of the divine command, is of sufficient power to bring about everything that must be effected by divine power concerning some body beyond natural operations (to which alone angels are sent), it cannot be that the operations of two angels immediately converge on the same object; therefore two angels cannot be in the same place, since one of them would be superfluous — just as the philosophers, following Aristotle, attributed only one mover to each celestial sphere.
claims: Angels are 'in one place' univocally with all beings only in the metaphorical sense of being contained in God; the question concerns proper, corporeal place.

It is impossible for the same effect to be produced immediately by two agents each independently sufficient for the whole effect, since a perfect agent leaves nothing further for another agent to actualize.

Because one angel's power, exercised by divine command, is fully sufficient for whatever it is sent to do to a body, two angels cannot immediately operate on the same object — hence two angels cannot occupy the same place, since one would be redundant.
This parallels the Aristotelian principle that only one mover is assigned to each celestial sphere.
concepts: God as metaphorical place of all beings

ta-l1d37q3-d1e256.summary: Reply to the first objection. It is not the mere filling of place that prevents several angels from being simultaneously in one place, but rather the confusion of operations, which would in some way redound into a confusion of power and essence.
claims: The barrier to angelic co-location is operational confusion (and its implications for power and essence), not spatial 'crowding' as such.
concepts: confusion of operations vs. mere spatial occupation

ta-l1d37q3-d1e259.summary: Reply to the second objection. The soul is in the body as a form giving esse and performing natural operations, whereas an angel is in a body as performing supernatural operations; since these operations are not of the same ratio (kind), no confusion of operations arises between an indwelling soul and an indwelling angel or demon.
claims: A soul and an angel/demon can co-occupy a body without confusion because their operations differ in kind — natural, esse-giving operation versus supernatural operation — unlike the case of two angels.

ta-l1d37q3-d1e263.summary: This also resolves the third objection: God is in things as giving esse to all of them and operating within any operative power they have, so his operation is of a wholly different ratio (kind) from that of an angel; hence no confusion follows from angels being 'within' God, and this case does not support the co-location of two angels, whose operations would be of the same kind.
claims: Angels' unconfused presence 'within' God does not license angel-angel co-location, since God's esse-giving, all-encompassing operation differs in kind from any angel's operation, unlike the case of two angels acting on the same object.
concepts: difference in kind (ratio) as what prevents confusion

ta-l1d37q3-d1e266.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. As is commonly said, an illuminating angel does not operate within the essence of the illuminated angel, since it is not the cause of that angel's esse, and the light it imparts is not received into the illuminated angel's esse; it is therefore said to operate, as it were, externally, by way of suggestion. Similarly, although an angel's effect on a body is not received into the body's esse (of which the angel is not the cause), it is received within the body's dimensions, by reason of which the angel can be called intrinsic to the body — but this cannot be said of its relation to a soul or to another angel; hence it does not follow that an illuminating angel is 'in' or 'with' the illuminated angel in one place.
claims: Angelic illumination is an external, suggestive operation that does not enter the illuminated angel's esse, unlike an angel's operation on a body, which is received within the body's dimensions.

Because an angel can be called 'intrinsic' to a body it acts on (via reception within its dimensions) but not to another angel or a soul, the illumination objection fails to establish that two angels can share one place.
concepts: reception within dimensions vs. within esse

ta-l1d37q3-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium to Quaestio 3, a single paragraph locating this question within Lombard's text (the exclusion from God of locality and motion, properties that follow on a creature's existing in place) and identifying the three articles on angelic place: whether an angel is in place, whether one angel can be in several places at once, and whether several angels can be in one place.
concepts: locality and motion as excluded from God

ta-l1d37q3-Dd1e123.summary: Article 1 asks whether an angel is in place. Six objections deny it, appealing to Boethius's dictum that incorporeal things are not in place, the per-accidens presence proper to what is free of dimension, the impossibility of attributing 'in place' to operation itself, the apparent absurdity of angels being 'nowhere' when not operating on bodies, the implication that God too would be definitively located if operation-based presence entailed definitive location, and philosophical precedent (separate intelligences, Plato's Ideas) for operating on located things without being in place. The sed contra appeals to liturgical and patristic authority (the collect, Damascene). In the respondeo, Thomas surveys three opinions — the heretical philosophical denial of any angelic relation to place, a crude 'finite essence entails finite place' argument resting on an equivocation, and his own (and Gregory Nazianzen's) view that an angel is in place solely through operation, in three possible modes (conferring something added to esse, conferring an esse other than its own, or conferring its own esse as form or as hypostasis). The replies consistently distinguish 'in place as in place' (which never applies to angels except per accidens, through an assumed or affected body) from 'in place as operator in what is operated on' (which applies to angels per se), resolve the apparent absurdity of angelic non-location as merely non-imaginable rather than impossible, distinguish God's operation (place-determined only at its terminus, not its origin, since God acts everywhere at once) from an angel's (place-determined at both ends), and show that the philosophers' denial of place to intelligences rests on their own doctrine of merely mediated operation, not on a general truth.
claims: An angel is in place only through its operation, never as a measured or contained thing (in the sense proper to bodies), and only per se in the distinct sense of operator-in-operated.

God differs from an angel in being place-determined, if at all, only at the terminus of operation, never at its origin, since he acts everywhere simultaneously; an angel's operation is place-determined at both origin and terminus.
concepts: esse as act of form vs. hypostasis

ta-l1d37q3-Dd1e182.summary: Article 2 asks whether an angel can be in several places at once. Four objections argue for multi-location by analogy with Christ's Eucharistic body, from an angel's immediate motion of every part of an assumed body, from an angel's continuous contemplation in the empyrean heaven even while operating elsewhere, and from an angel's power exceeding any single object it acts on. Two sed contra arguments appeal to Damascene and to the prior article's establishment of definitive presence. In the respondeo, Thomas rejects both the view that angels can be in several (but not all) places and the view that an angel occupies an indivisible point-place (diagnosed as an imagination-bound error), holding instead that an angel occupies exactly one place, whose extent is fixed by the immediate terminus of its single operation, because a finite power can sustain only one operation terminating in one object — unlike God, whose infinite power grounds a single, self-identical operation with infinite effects, making him present in many places, indeed all places, at once. The replies clarify that Christ's Eucharistic multi-location stems from transubstantiation and persisting accidents, not from any property of angelic or bodily presence as such; that presence in every part of one assumed body counts as one place, since one operation covers it as a whole; that place belongs to an angel's operation by its terminus (the object), not its origin, so a spiritual object of contemplation requires no corporeal place, and the empyrean heaven is only fittingly, not necessarily, angels' 'place' of contemplation; and that an angel's excess of power over its object is an excess of magnitude, not of number, so it cannot license simultaneous operation on multiple objects.
claims: An angel occupies exactly one place at a time, whose size is determined entirely by the immediate terminus of its single operation, because a finite power supports only one operation terminating in one object.
Only God, whose infinite power grounds one self-identical operation with infinite effects, can be present in many or all places simultaneously.
concepts: finite power admits only one operation
unity of place via unity of operation

ta-l1d37q3-Dd1e226.summary: Article 3 asks whether several angels can be in one place. Four objections argue for co-location: bodies (which fill place more fully than spirits) do not exclude an angel, so a fortiori another angel should not either; demons and angels can co-occupy a body already animated by a soul; the greater ontological distinction between created and uncreated spirit does not prevent angels from being 'within' God without confusion, so the lesser distinction between two created spirits should allow co-location even more readily; and an illuminating angel's operation on another angel should, by the operation-based criterion of presence, place it 'in' that angel. Two sed contra arguments draw analogies to the impossibility of two bodies sharing a circumscribed place and of one body having two souls. In the respondeo, Thomas distinguishes the metaphorical 'place' of angels in God (in which all beings coincide) from proper corporeal place, and argues, on the principle that a perfect agent exhausts its patient's potency, that two angels cannot immediately operate on the same object, since one angel's divinely-empowered operation is already fully sufficient — making a second angel superfluous, just as Aristotelian cosmology assigns only one mover per sphere. The replies clarify that the true barrier is confusion of operations, not mere spatial occupation; that a soul and an angel can co-occupy a body without confusion because their operations differ in kind (natural/esse-giving versus supernatural); that God's esse-giving, all-encompassing operation likewise differs in kind from any angel's, so angels' unconfused presence 'within' God does not license angel-angel co-location; and that angelic illumination is an external, suggestive operation that does not enter the illuminated angel's esse (unlike an angel's effect on a body, received within its dimensions), so it does not place one angel 'in' another.
claims: Two angels cannot occupy the same proper (corporeal) place, because a perfect agent's operation exhausts its patient's potency, leaving nothing for a second angel's operation to actualize — a second angel would be superfluous.

Co-location without confusion is possible only between operations differing in kind (as a soul's natural operation differs from an angel's supernatural one, or God's esse-giving operation differs from any angel's), which is why the soul-angel and angel-in-God cases do not establish that two angels of the same kind of operation could share a place.

ta-l1d37q3.summary: Quaestio 3 of Distinction 37 takes up angelic place and motion, the two conditions that follow upon a creature's existing in place, having already excluded them from God (locality and motion are excluded from God in principle in the Prooemium and treated for bodies by natural philosophy, not theology). It divides into a Prooemium and three articles on angelic place (motion is deferred). Article 1 establishes that an angel is in place solely through its operation — as operator in what is operated on, not as a measured, contained thing — and in exactly the graded way appropriate to a finite spiritual substance able to confer something added to esse, an esse other than its own, or (uniquely in the Incarnation) its own esse as act of hypostasis. Article 2 shows that an angel, having finite power capable of only one operation terminating in one object, occupies exactly one place at a time (of whatever size its immediate operation covers), in contrast to God, whose infinite power and single, self-identical yet infinitely effective operation makes him present in many places, indeed all places, at once. Article 3 shows that two angels cannot occupy the same proper (corporeal) place, because one angel's divinely-empowered operation already exhausts what can be done to a given object, leaving no work — and so no place — for a second angel of the same kind of operation, whereas co-location without confusion (as of a soul and an angel, or of angels 'within' God) is possible only between operations that differ in kind.
claims: An angel is in place only through operation (as operator in operated), a mode of presence graded by what it confers (something added to esse, another's esse, or its own esse), and always confined to exactly one place at a time because its power, being finite, sustains only one operation terminating in one object.

Divine omnipresence and angelic single-location differ precisely because God's power and self-identical operation are infinite, while an angel's are finite — and this same finitude explains why two angels of the same kind of operation cannot share one place, since a sufficient agent's operation leaves nothing for a second agent of like kind to do.
